crashapi

The goal of the crashapi R package is to provide functions for downloading data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) API.

What is FARS? NHTSA explains: “The Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) contains data on all vehicle crashes in the United States that occur on a public roadway and involve a fatality.”

Installation

You can install the development version of crashapi using the pak package:

pak::pkg_install("elipousson/crashapi")

Background

Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) API support

Supported APIs for this package include:

Most of these APIs support XML, JSV, CSV, and JSON output formats. This package only uses JSON with the exception of get_fars_year() (which supports downloading CSV files).

For reference, this package also includes a list of terms and NHTSA technical definitions in fars_terms and a list of variable labels in fars_vars_labels.

The FARS API currently provides access to data from 2010 to 2024. The NHTSA website also provides additional information on the release data and version status for the FARS data files available through the API:

Data Year File Version Release Date
2010 Final December 11, 2012
2011 Final November 13, 2013
2012 Final December 12, 2013
2013 Final December 14, 2014
2014 Final December 18, 2015
2015 Final December 16, 2016
2016 Final December 14, 2017
2017 Final December 18, 2018
2018 Final June 24, 2021
2019 Final March 2, 2022
2020 Final April 3, 2023
2021 Final April 1, 2024
2022 Final April 8, 2025
2023 Final April 1, 2026
2024 Annual April 1, 2026

Changes to the sex variable

According to the Data Index terminations tracker, in February 2025 NHTSA renamed the person-level gender variable to “Sex” and recoded its third response value to “Not Reported”, removing the non-binary category from published FARS data files. The FARS 2022 release notes confirm that on February 11, 2025, NHTSA replaced attribute 3 with attribute 8 (Not Reported), updating 22 records in the PERSON table and 1 record in the PBTYPE table. See OMB ICR 202503-2127-008 and the Williams Institute report Removal of SOGI from Federal Data Collections (Feb 2026) for more information.

Data now returned by the CrashAPI codes SEX as 1 (Male), 2 (Female), 8 (Not Reported), or 9 (Reported as Unknown) for all years, so people previously recorded as non-binary now appear as “Not Reported”.

Additional data access functionality

The get_fars_zip() function can be used to access FARS data files from 1975 to 2024 that are not available via the API but are available for download through the NHTSA File Downloads site as zipped CSV or SAS files. Zipped CSV files are converted to parquet files and cached in the user cache directory (see tools::R_user_dir()) so the data only needs to be downloaded once. This site also provides extensive technical documentation on coding and use of the FARS data files.

The get_crss_zip() function works the same way for data files from the Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS) from 2016 to 2024. CRSS is a national sample of police-reported crashes of all severities (not only fatal crashes) that replaced the General Estimates System (GES) in 2016. Since CRSS is a sample, national estimates should use the sampling weights and survey design variables described in the CRSS Analytical User’s Manual, and the data does not include crash locations.

Earlier data along with data from the General Estimates System (GES) / Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS) is also available through the Fatality and Injury Reporting System Tool (FIRST).

Examples 

library(crashapi)
library(ggplot2)

Use get_fars() to get a FARS data table (e.g. accident, person, or vehicle) for one or more states, a county, and one or more years. Data for a state from 2010 onwards comes from the CrashAPI and national data or data before 2010 comes from the cached zipped data files.

# Get the person table for Baltimore City, MD for 2022
md_people <-
  get_fars(
    state = "MD",
    county = "Baltimore city",
    year = 2022,
    type = "person"
  )

head(md_people[, c("ST_CASE", "VEH_NO", "PER_NO", "AGE", "SEXNAME", "INJ_SEVNAME")])
#>     ST_CASE VEH_NO PER_NO AGE SEXNAME            INJ_SEVNAME
#> 133  240061      0      1  58    Male       Fatal Injury (K)
#> 134  240061      1      1  32    Male No Apparent Injury (O)
#> 163  240071      0      1  57    Male       Fatal Injury (K)
#> 164  240071      1      1  37  Female No Apparent Injury (O)
#> 165  240072      0      1  55    Male       Fatal Injury (K)
#> 166  240072      1      1  30    Male No Apparent Injury (O)

You can set geometry to TRUE to convert the accident table into an sf object for mapping.

crashes_sf <-
  get_fars(
    state = "NC",
    county = "Wake County",
    year = 2018:2021,
    geometry = TRUE
  )
#> ℹ Requesting data for all years from 2018 to 2021, including 2019 and 2020 not
#>   in `year`.

nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"))
#> Reading layer `nc' from data source 
#>   `/Users/elipousson/Library/R/arm64/4.6/library/sf/shape/nc.shp' 
#>   using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
#> Simple feature collection with 100 features and 14 fields
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -84.32385 ymin: 33.88199 xmax: -75.45698 ymax: 36.58965
#> Geodetic CRS:  NAD27
wake_co <- sf::st_transform(nc[nc$NAME == "Wake", ], 4326)

# Map crashes
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = wake_co,
    fill = NA,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = sf::st_crop(crashes_sf, wake_co),
    aes(color = VE_TOTAL),
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  theme_void()
#> Warning in st_is_longlat(x): bounding box has potentially an invalid value
#> range for longlat data
#> Warning in st_is_longlat(x): bounding box has potentially an invalid value
#> range for longlat data
#> Warning: attribute variables are assumed to be spatially constant throughout
#> all geometries

National data or data before 2010 is downloaded and cached the first time it is used:

# Get the national vehicle table for 2024
get_fars(year = 2024, type = "vehicle")

# Get the accident table for Maryland for 2005
get_fars(state = "MD", year = 2005)

CRSS data files can be downloaded and cached with get_crss_zip():

# Get all CRSS tables for 2024
crss_2024 <- get_crss_zip(year = 2024)

# Estimate the number of police-reported crashes using the sampling weight
sum(crss_2024$accident$WEIGHT)

Other CrashAPI endpoints are available through specific functions. For example, you can use get_fars_summary() to access state-level summary data on crash and fatality counts.

# Get summary crash count and fatality count data for Maryland from 2010 to 2021
md_summary <- get_fars_summary(state = "MD", year = 2010:2021)

ggplot(md_summary, aes(x = CaseYear, y = TotalFatalCounts)) +
  geom_point(color = "red") +
  geom_line(color = "red", group = 1) +
  theme_minimal()

You can list crashes and filter by the number of vehicles involved with get_fars_crash_list().

# Get fatal crashes in New York state from 2019 with 5 to 10 vehicles
get_fars_crash_list(state = "NY", year = 2019, vehicles = c(5, 10))

If you call get_fars_crashes() with details set to TRUE, additional information from get_fars_cases() (including the crash date and time) is appended to the crash data frame.

# Get fatal crashes for Anne Arundel County, MD for 2019 and append details
crashes_detailed <-
  get_fars_crashes(
    state = "MD",
    county = "Anne Arundel County",
    year = 2019,
    details = TRUE
  )
#> ■■■■■■■■■                         28% | ETA:  9s
#> ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■          78% | ETA:  3s

# Show 10 fatal crashes at random
dplyr::slice_sample(crashes_detailed, n = 10)

Related packages and projects

  • rfars aims to “simplify the process of analyzing FARS data” by providing access to FARS downloads and preprocessed data back to 2015.
  • stats19 “provides functions for downloading and formatting road crash data” from “the UK’s official road traffic casualty database, STATS19.”
  • njtr1: “An R interface to New Jersey traffic crash data reported on form NJTR-1.”
  • wisdotcrashdatabase: “A package used for internal WisDOT crash database pulls and analysis.”
  • nzcrash: “An R package to distribute New Zealand crash data in a convenient form.”
  • GraphHopper Open Traffic Collection: “Collections of URLs pointing to traffic information portals which contain open data or at least data which is free to use.”
  • Open Crash Data Index: A Google Sheet listing a range of city, county, regional and state sources for crash data including non-injury crashes as well as the fatal crashes available through the FARS API. Contributions for crash data from other U.S. cities and states are welcome.
